title: Establish Accounts: Cloud Accounts
summary: Cloud accounts give an adversary storage, compute and messaging capacity without owning a single server, and they are usually obtained through a self-service sign-up that needs only a mailbox and a payment method. The same tenant can stage exfiltration in object storage, serve tooling, run virtual machines or serverless functions, and send bulk mail through notification or email services whose domains carry strong sender reputation. Because the provisioning is legitimate, the visible traces are commercial rather than malicious: subscriptions with no corporate billing history, buckets written to shortly after sign-up, compute started outside working hours, and messaging quotas burned far faster than a normal trial would. This sub-technique covers cloud tenancies specifically, not online accounts in general.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker opens an account with a cloud company. Cloud companies rent storage, computers and messaging services over the internet. The attacker pays a small amount or uses a free trial. They then have powerful tools without owning any hardware. The parent technique covers all accounts, but this part is only about cloud providers and what they rent out.
beginner.whyItMatters: Cloud accounts are quick to open and hard to trace back. Stolen data can be stored in them, and malicious files can be served from them. Messages sent through a cloud provider often pass spam filters because the provider's name is trusted. An attacker can also run many machines for a short time and then delete them. If you never look at what your own cloud tenants are doing, you may host an attacker's work without knowing it. Account and billing reviews matter as much as network monitoring.
howItWorks: The attacker registers a cloud account, usually with an email address and a payment card.
They may start with a free trial to test storage, computing or messaging limits.
They create storage space and upload tools or stolen files into it.
They run virtual machines or small functions to carry their attack traffic.
They use the provider's messaging service to send large amounts of mail.
When the work is done, they delete the resources so little remains behind.
beginner.example: Imagine a self-storage site where you can rent a locker with a bank card and no questions asked. You get a key the same afternoon. Some people store furniture. Others use the locker to hold things they do not want found, and they empty it before anyone looks. Cloud accounts are those lockers. The key is a credit card and an email address. The company running the site is honest, but it cannot see what every locker holds.
takeaways: Cloud services are rented in minutes, so abuse can start very quickly.
Watch for storage or computing resources that appear and disappear fast.
Keep your own cloud keys locked down and review who uses them.

objectives: Describe how cloud accounts provide storage, compute and messaging to an adversary.
Explain the difference between this sub-technique and its parent technique.
Identify billing and resource logs that reveal short-lived cloud abuse.
Recognise how provider reputation helps malicious mail avoid filters.
Recommend access controls that protect legitimate cloud tenants.
